meta.title: Patient Care: Pressure Injuries, Falls, and Mobility
meta.title_en: Patient Care: Pressure Injuries, Falls, and Mobility

lessons.title: Pressure Injury Prevention and Staging
lessons.lay_summary: Pressure injuries (bedsores) develop when skin is compressed against a hard surface for too long. They are largely preventable. Nurses use risk tools and frequent repositioning to protect vulnerable patients.

content.intro: Pressure injuries are a nursing-sensitive outcome — their prevalence reflects the quality of nursing care. They cause pain, prolong hospitalisation, increase mortality, and represent a failure of preventive care.

sections.title: Pressure Injury Risk Assessment
sections.body:
Braden Scale is the most validated risk assessment tool (adults). Six subscales scored 1–3 or 4: Sensory perception, Moisture, Activity, Mobility, Nutrition, Friction and shear. Total score: 6–23. Higher score = lower risk.
Cut-offs vary by setting: ≤18 = at risk; ≤13 = high risk; ≤9 = very high risk.
Assess on admission and at minimum every 24 hours or with any significant change in condition. Other validated tools: Waterlow (UK), Norton.

sections.title: NPIAP Pressure Injury Stages
sections.body:
Stage 1: Non-blanchable redness of intact skin. Red area does not turn white when pressed for 3 seconds. No skin break.
Stage 2: Partial-thickness skin loss. Shallow open wound (pink/red wound bed) or intact/ruptured serum-filled blister. No adipose tissue visible.
Stage 3: Full-thickness skin loss. Adipose tissue visible. May have slough and/or eschar. Tunnelling/undermining possible.
Stage 4: Full-thickness tissue loss with exposed bone, tendon, or muscle. Often have tunnelling/undermining. Highest risk of osteomyelitis.
Unstageable: full-thickness with slough/eschar obscuring the wound bed — cannot determine depth until debrided.
Deep Tissue Pressure Injury (DTPI): intact skin with persistent non-blanchable deep red/maroon/purple discolouration, or blood-filled blister. Results from intense/prolonged pressure at bone-tissue interface.

sections.title: Prevention Strategies
sections.body:
1. Repositioning: minimum every 2 hours in bed (30° lateral tilt preferred — reduces pressure on trochanter vs 90° lateral); every 15 min in wheelchair.
2. Pressure-redistributing surfaces: specialty foam mattress (minimum for at-risk); alternating-pressure mattress for high risk.
3. Skin care: keep skin clean and dry; use moisturiser on at-risk areas; avoid massage over bony prominences.
4. Nutrition: adequate protein (1.2–1.5 g/kg/day for at-risk patients); vitamin C and zinc supplementation if deficient; refer to dietitian.
5. Microclimate: moisture from incontinence is a major risk factor — use barrier creams, absorbent pads, catheter for faecal incontinence if appropriate.
6. Heel offloading: elevate heels off mattress with foam heel protectors or a pillow under the lower legs.

content.clinical_pearl: Stage 1 is reversible if caught and pressure relieved. Once Stage 2 occurs, healing takes weeks. Stage 4 may take months or years, require surgery, and may be fatal in frail patients. Prevention is always more effective than treatment. Document skin assessment on admission as a legal baseline.
key_points: Braden Scale: ≤18 at risk; ≤13 high risk; assess every 24 h
Stage 1: non-blanchable redness (intact skin) — most important to catch
Reposition minimum every 2 hours; 30° lateral tilt preferred
Heels must be offloaded — they are the second most common pressure injury site after sacrum
Document skin status on admission as legal baseline
references: EPUAP/NPIAP/PPPIA Prevention and Treatment of Pressure Ulcers 2019

lessons.title: Falls Prevention and Safe Patient Handling

content.intro: Falls are the most common adverse event in hospitals. One-third of in-hospital falls result in injury; 10% result in serious injury (fractures, head trauma). They are largely preventable with systematic risk assessment and individualised interventions.

sections.title: Falls Risk Assessment
sections.body:
Validated tools: Morse Fall Scale (most commonly used in hospitals); STRATIFY; Hendrich II.
Morse Fall Scale: history of falling (25 pts), secondary diagnosis (15), ambulatory aid (0–30), IV/heparin lock (20), gait (0–20), mental status (0–15). Score ≥45 = high risk; 25–44 = moderate risk; 0–24 = low risk.
Assess on admission, after a fall, and at change in condition. Falls risk is dynamic — re-assess with medication changes, post-procedure, postoperative, or new confusion.

sections.title: Universal and High-Risk Interventions
sections.body:
Universal (all patients): call bell within reach; bed in lowest position; wheels locked; non-slip footwear; adequate lighting; clear path to bathroom.
High-risk (Morse ≥45): yellow non-slip socks/arm band; 'Falls Risk' signage on door/bed (with patient consent); hourly rounding; offer toileting every 2 h; bed/chair alarm; low bed; floor mat if appropriate; supervised ambulation only; review and withhold high-risk medications (opioids, benzodiazepines, diuretics at night, antihypertensives — check with physician).
Post-fall: assess for injury; vital signs; neurological assessment if head involved; document; notify physician; complete incident report; fall huddle within 24 h.

sections.title: Safe Patient Handling and Mobility
sections.body:
Nurses have among the highest rates of musculoskeletal injury of any profession due to manual patient handling. Safe patient handling principles: Use mechanical lifts for patients who cannot weight bear (Hoyer lift). Use transfer belts for patients who can assist. Never lift from the floor alone — use a team or lift device. Assess mobility level before each transfer (0 = totally dependent → 5 = independent — ANA Mobility Scale).
Early mobility reduces hospital-acquired pressure injuries, pneumonia, DVT, delirium, and deconditioning. Engage physiotherapy early. Encourage patients to sit out of bed by day 1 post-op where possible.

content.clinical_pearl: The most dangerous time for falls is nighttime (unfamiliar environment, poor lighting, medication effects) and during toileting (urgency, standing up quickly). Proactive toileting (offer every 2 hours) reduces falls by 20–30% in high-risk patients.
key_points: Morse Fall Scale ≥45 = high risk; implement high-risk bundle immediately
Most falls occur during toileting and at night — proactive toileting is evidence-based prevention
Universal precautions apply to ALL patients regardless of risk score
Use mechanical lift devices for fully dependent patients — never lift alone
After any fall: assess, document, incident report, physician notification, team huddle
references: NICE NG15 Falls Prevention in Older People 2023
ANA Safe Patient Handling and Mobility 2013

lessons.title: Wound Assessment and Evidence-Based Wound Care
lessons.lay_summary: Wound assessment guides dressing choice. Choosing the wrong dressing delays healing. Systematic documentation is also a medicolegal requirement.

content.intro: Wound management is one of the most common nursing activities, yet significant variation in practice exists. Evidence-based wound care requires systematic assessment using validated tools, appropriate dressing selection based on wound characteristics, and clear documentation that enables continuity of care.

sections.title: Wound Assessment: TIME Framework
sections.body: TIME (Wound Bed Preparation framework, Dowsett & Newton 2000): T — Tissue: what types? Granulation (healthy, red, moist — promotes healing), Slough (yellow, soft — devitalised, inhibits healing), Eschar (black, hard — devitalised, remove unless dry/stable on diabetic foot), Epithelising (pink, at wound edge — indicates healing). I — Infection/Inflammation: signs of infection: increased pain, erythema extending >2 cm beyond wound edge, warmth, swelling, purulent exudate, malodour, friable granulation, failure to progress in 2+ weeks. Wound swab for culture (superficial swab often non-diagnostic — tissue biopsy or Levine technique preferred). M — Moisture: exudate level (none/dry, minimal, moderate, heavy) guides dressing absorbency. E — Edge: advancing (epithelialisation occurring), non-advancing (wound stalled), rolled/undermined (creates pocket — requires exploration).

sections.title: Dressing Selection Principles
sections.body: Dry wound: hydrate (hydrogel, hydrocolloid — maintain moist wound environment). Wet/high exudate: absorb (foam, alginate, hydrofibre — prevent maceration). Infected wound: antimicrobial (silver-containing dressings — silver sulfadiazine, silver foam; honey-impregnated — Medihoney; iodine — Inadine). Necrotic/sloughy: debridement (hydrogel for autolytic debridement; enzymatic; surgical/sharp — by trained clinician). Granulating wound: protect and maintain moisture (foam, non-adherent). Epithelialising wound: protect and minimise trauma (thin film, non-adherent). Key principle: moist wound environment (Winter 1962) accelerates healing 40% vs dry healing. Do NOT use: dry gauze on granulating wounds (damages healing tissue on removal), hydrogen peroxide (cytotoxic to healing cells), 'traditional' wound lotions without evidence base.

content.clinical_pearl: A wound that is not progressing after 2-4 weeks of appropriate management needs reassessment — not just a different dressing. Consider: Is there underlying infection? Is perfusion adequate (check ABPIs in chronic leg ulcers)? Is the patient nutritionally replete? Are there systemic factors (diabetes, steroids)? Escalate to tissue viability specialist.
key_points: TIME framework: Tissue, Infection/Inflammation, Moisture, Edge
Moist wound environment: accelerates healing 40% vs dry
Silver/honey/iodine dressings for infected wounds; hydrogel for dry/necrotic
Non-healing wound at 2-4 weeks: reassess for infection, perfusion, nutrition, systemic factors
Hydrogen peroxide and dry gauze on granulating tissue: evidence-based contraindications
references: Dowsett C & Newton H. Wound bed preparation: TIME in practice. Wounds UK 2005;1(3):58-70
NICE. Guideline NG19: Pressure ulcers prevention and management. NICE, 2014
Winter GD. Formation of scab and rate of epithelisation of superficial wounds. Nature 1962;193:293-294

lessons.title: Nutritional Support and Malnutrition Screening
lessons.lay_summary: Malnutrition is present in up to 40% of hospitalised patients and is associated with delayed wound healing, higher infection rates, and longer hospital stays. Nurses screen, identify, and initiate nutritional support.

content.intro: Malnutrition is defined as a deficiency, excess, or imbalance of energy, protein, or other nutrients causing measurable adverse effects on body composition, function, or clinical outcomes. In hospitalised adults, it is associated with 3× higher mortality, increased infection rates, impaired wound healing, and prolonged hospital stay. The MUST (Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool) is the validated tool recommended by BAPEN and NICE.

sections.title: MUST Screening Tool
sections.body: MUST is a five-step screening tool recommended for screening in all healthcare settings (NICE CG32, BAPEN). Step 1: BMI score (>20 = 0; 18.5-20 = 1; <18.5 = 2). Step 2: unplanned weight loss in past 3-6 months (BMI) (5-10% = 1; >10% = 2). Step 3: acute disease effect score (if acutely ill and no or very little intake for >5 days likely = 2). Step 4: add scores (total 0 = low risk; 1 = medium risk; ≥2 = high risk). Step 5: management guideline. Low risk: routine screening. Medium risk: observe (document diet intake 3 days; dietitian referral if intake inadequate). High risk: treat (refer dietitian; supplemental nutrition support — ONS first, then enteral, then parenteral).

sections.title: Nutritional Support: Oral, Enteral, Parenteral
sections.body: Oral nutritional supplements (ONS): high-protein/calorie sip feeds if patient can eat and swallow safely. Enteral nutrition (EN): nasogastric (NG) or nasojejunal (NJ) tube feeding; gastrostomy (PEG/RIG) for long-term; preferred route when GI tract functional. Nursing NG tube care: confirm position before each feed and medication (pH ≤5.5 on aspirate, or CXR if no aspirate); head-of-bed elevation ≥30° during feeding (reduces aspiration); check residual volume (withhold feed if >200-250 mL); flush 30 mL water before and after medications and every 4-6h. Parenteral: see TPN module (NURSE-003). Benefits of enteral over parenteral: maintains gut mucosal integrity (prevents bacterial translocation), lower infection rate, lower cost, physiological.

content.clinical_pearl: Confirm NG tube position before EVERY use — even if the tube hasn't been touched since the last confirmed check. Tube position can migrate without obvious signs. pH ≤5.5 from aspirate is the first-line method; X-ray is required when no aspirate can be obtained after appropriate manoeuvres. Feeding into a misplaced tube causes aspiration pneumonia — frequently fatal.
key_points: MUST ≥2 = high risk; refer dietitian; supplement orally, then enteral, then parenteral
Enteral nutrition preferred when GI tract functional — maintains mucosal integrity
NG tube: confirm position with pH ≤5.5 before EVERY use, or CXR if no aspirate
HOB ≥30° during NG feeding; flush with 30 mL water q4-6h
Malnutrition in hospital: ×3 mortality, delayed wound healing, increased infections
references: BAPEN. The MUST Explanatory Booklet. BAPEN, 2011
NICE. Guideline NG22: Nutrition support for adults. NICE, 2006 updated 2017
NHS England. Patient safety alert: nasogastric tube misplacement. 2012, updated 2016

flashcards.question: Name the 6 Braden Scale subscales.
flashcards.answer: Sensory perception, Moisture, Activity, Mobility, Nutrition, Friction and shear. Higher score = lower pressure injury risk.

flashcards.question: What characterises a Stage 1 pressure injury?
flashcards.answer: Non-blanchable erythema of intact skin. The red area does NOT turn white when pressed for 3 seconds. No break in skin.

flashcards.question: Repositioning frequency for a bed-bound patient?
flashcards.answer: Minimum every 2 hours; 30-degree lateral tilt is preferred over 90-degree to reduce trochanter pressure.

flashcards.question: Morse Fall Scale score for high risk?
flashcards.answer: ≥45 points = high risk. Implement full falls prevention bundle.

flashcards.question: Two most common pressure injury sites in hospitalised patients?
flashcards.answer: Sacrum/coccyx (most common) and heels (second most common). Both require dedicated offloading.

mcq_questions.question: A Braden Scale assessment reveals a total score of 12 for a 78-year-old patient admitted after a stroke. Which response is most appropriate?

options.A: Reposition every 4 hours; standard hospital mattress is adequate
options.B: Initiate a high-risk pressure injury prevention bundle including specialty mattress, 2-hourly repositioning, skin assessment, and dietitian referral
options.C: Score indicates low risk — routine care only
options.D: Apply a stage 1 dressing to the sacrum prophylactically

mcq_questions.explanation: Braden score 12 is ≤13 = high risk. This requires the full prevention bundle: specialty pressure-redistribution surface (alternating pressure or high-specification foam), 2-hourly repositioning (30° tilt), full skin assessment, heels elevated, nutritional assessment/dietitian referral. Score 12 is NOT low risk.

mcq_questions.question: Select ALL nursing actions that are included in the universal falls prevention bundle (for ALL patients, regardless of falls risk score).

options.A: Ensure call bell is within reach
options.C: Bed in lowest safe position with wheels locked
options.F: Clear unobstructed path to the bathroom

mcq_questions.explanation: Universal bundle (all patients): call bell in reach (A), bed lowest and locked (C), non-slip footwear (E), clear path to bathroom (F). Yellow armband (B) and hourly rounding (D) are high-risk interventions, not universal.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse inspects the sacrum of an 85-year-old bed-bound patient and notes an area of persistent redness that does NOT blanch when pressed for 3 seconds. The skin is intact. How should this be staged and managed?

options.A: Stage 2 — apply a moist wound dressing
options.B: Stage 1 — relieve pressure immediately; document; increase repositioning frequency; apply barrier film if skin fragile
options.D: Deep Tissue Pressure Injury — arrange urgent surgical review

mcq_questions.explanation: Non-blanchable erythema of intact skin = Stage 1 pressure injury. It is reversible if pressure is relieved immediately. Stage 2 requires skin breakdown. Unstageable requires wound covered with slough/eschar. DTPI presents with persistent deep red/maroon/purple or blood-filled blister, usually over a bony prominence.

mcq_questions.question: A patient scores 14 on the Braden Scale. How would you interpret this score and what action is required?

options.A: No risk — no pressure injury prevention needed
options.B: Mild risk — implement a repositioning schedule every 2 hours and moisture management
options.C: Moderate risk — initiate full pressure injury prevention protocol
options.D: High risk — place in ICU for continuous monitoring

mcq_questions.explanation: Braden Scale interpretation: 19–23 = no risk; 15–18 = mild risk; 13–14 = moderate risk; 10–12 = high risk; ≤9 = very high risk. A score of 14 = moderate risk, requiring a full prevention bundle: 2-hourly repositioning, pressure-redistributing mattress, moisture management, nutritional support, and wound assessment.

mcq_questions.question: A Stage 2 pressure injury is characterised by:

options.B: Partial-thickness skin loss with exposed dermis — no slough or eschar
options.C: Full-thickness skin loss with visible fat
options.D: Full-thickness skin loss reaching fascia, muscle, or bone

mcq_questions.explanation: NPIAP/EPUAP Pressure Injury Staging: Stage 1 = non-blanchable redness on intact skin; Stage 2 = partial-thickness loss exposing dermis (moist wound, intact or ruptured blister); Stage 3 = full-thickness loss with visible subcutaneous fat; Stage 4 = full-thickness loss reaching muscle/bone/tendon.

mcq_questions.question: An 80-year-old patient with a hip fracture is admitted to the orthopaedic ward. Which fall prevention intervention is the HIGHEST priority?

options.A: Place a fall-risk bracelet on the patient's wrist
options.B: Keep the bed at the lowest position with side rails up and call bell within reach
options.C: Tell the patient not to get up without calling for help
options.D: Document the fall risk in the nursing notes

mcq_questions.explanation: Environmental safety modifications — lowest bed height, appropriate use of side rails, call bell within reach, non-slip footwear, and clear pathways — are the highest-priority physical interventions to prevent falls. Patient education (C) and documentation (D) are important but secondary to creating a safe environment.

mcq_questions.question: When repositioning a bedridden patient to prevent pressure injuries, how frequently should turns occur (minimum standard)?
mcq_questions.explanation: Clinical guidelines (EPUAP/NPIAP/PPPIA 2019) recommend repositioning at least every 2 hours for patients at risk of pressure injury on standard mattresses. On high-specification foam mattresses, intervals may be extended to every 4 hours with monitoring. However, the universal standard minimum is every 2 hours.

mcq_questions.question: Which position should a nurse AVOID when repositioning a patient with a sacral pressure injury?

options.C: 90° side-lying directly on the hip (greater trochanter)

mcq_questions.explanation: 90° side-lying places maximum pressure on the greater trochanter — a bony prominence highly prone to pressure injury. The 30° tilted lateral position redistributes pressure away from bony prominences and is the preferred alternative. Prone and semi-prone positions remove sacral pressure entirely.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse uses a gait belt to assist an elderly patient from the bed to a chair. The patient begins to feel faint and their knees buckle. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Lower the patient to the floor in a controlled manner
options.B: Hold the patient upright until help arrives
options.C: Drag the patient back to the bed
options.D: Release the gait belt to call for help

mcq_questions.explanation: Controlled lowering to the floor protects both the patient from injury (a fall from height) and the nurse from back injury. Never attempt to hold a collapsing patient fully upright — doing so may cause both patient and nurse to fall. Once the patient is safely on the floor, call for assistance.

mcq_questions.question: Which heel protection strategy is most effective for preventing heel pressure injuries in bed-bound patients?

options.B: Regular massage of the heels with lotion
options.C: Heel elevation devices that float the heels off the bed surface

mcq_questions.explanation: Heel elevation devices (e.g., Heelift boots, pillows under the calf) completely offload pressure from the heel by suspending it above the mattress. Donut/ring devices paradoxically increase pressure at the wound margins. Massage is no longer recommended (can damage fragile tissue). Dressings protect but do not offload pressure.
